title: Impostor Syndrome: why founders feel like frauds and how Jason Cohen turned it into fuel
summary: Jason Cohen explains that feeling like a fraud is near-universal among high performers and founders, and that it comes from perfectionism rather than confidence. He separates constructive self-doubt, which drives learning and effort, from harmful doubt, which drives hiding and avoidance. He also gives concrete reframes for answering the inner voice.

principles.text: Founder drive comes from perfectionism and a need to do it your way, not from confidence that your way is right.
principles.quote: Our entrepreneurial motivation is not confidence, it's an insatiable desire to do it our way. Doing it our own way is not the same as being confident that it is the correct way.

principles.text: Self-doubt is useful when it pushes you to learn, fix and earn your reputation; harmful when it pushes you to hide or avoid.
principles.quote: I doubt my title as "expert," so every day I read, write, and immerse myself in my field.

principles.text: Emotions don't follow logic, so the fraud feeling persists even when the facts contradict it. Recognize it and deal with it logically.
principles.quote: Still, emotions don't respond to logic.

principles.text: When you doubt your skills, append "yet": you are a student on the way, not an impostor.
principles.quote: Whatever it is you think you're not good enough for, append the word "yet." I can't do this job... yet.

principles.text: Feeling stretched and unsure is the normal condition of anyone who strives, not proof you shouldn't be doing it.
principles.quote: That is the human condition... for humans who strive.

principles.text: Broad hands-on exposure can make you the real expert in a new field, even while you feel like a fraud.
principles.quote: I had developed more experience with more teams in more situations than any one person could
